chapter.title: Two Languages, One Stream
chapter.sub: The flood briefing reaches everyone — except the people who most need it.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 11 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT  The Brennock County EOC briefing room · Maya, Amara (accessibility lead), Imogen (PIO) and Director Oduya · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  The flood briefing goes out live at five. It reaches everyone — except the people listening in Spanish, the people who follow the interpreter, and the stations that carry it.  ⚑ RV-182: captions and interpretation are the accessibility lead’s. RV-183: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Two Languages, One Stream
items.stakes: The flood briefing is live — and it's shutting out Spanish speakers and people who rely on the interpreter.
items.clock: During today's briefing — and before tomorrow's.
items.reward: A briefing everyone it's for can follow, checked every time.

objectives.text: Find the copy on channel two
Decide how partners and lips get fixed

items.sub: Thursday · 5:02 p.m. · the briefing room, live

items.alt: The briefing room, the camera's red light on; Amara, the accessibility lead, points at the stream monitor above head height; Maya at the stream desk.

bubbles.text: We're live, and the people who most need this briefing are getting the worst of it.
Then we fix it live. Tell me what they're seeing.

items.caption: Live.

lines.text: We're live, and the people who most need this briefing are getting the worst of it.
Then we fix it live. Tell me what they're seeing.

items.text: Act I — “The copy on channel two”

items.prompt: 17:03, live. Channel two is English; the interpreter is out of frame. What do you do?
items.risk: Spanish speakers and sign-language users missing flood information.
timeout: The briefing ends in English only, interpreter unseen.

hints.text: What can be fixed on air — and who owns each fix?

options.label: Stop the stream until everything's fixed
options.result: Nobody gets the flood briefing, in any language.
options.consequence: Shuts everyone out instead of some.

options.label: Keep it live: route the interpreter to audio 2 now; ask the camera operator for a wider shot including the interpreter, with Amara confirming; tell Imogen so the county can say Spanish is back
options.result: Spanish on channel two in a minute; the interpreter in frame by 17:05; Imogen posts at 17:06 in both languages.
options.consequence: Fix what's yours live, with the owners, and tell the public.

options.label: Tell Spanish speakers to use automatic captions
options.result: Machine captions of English, for people who asked for Spanish.
options.consequence: A worse substitute for what they're owed.

options.label: Ask the interpreter to move closer to the podium
options.result: Amara: “She stands where she can see the speaker and be seen. The camera moves.”
options.consequence: Tells the interpreter how to do her job.
options.fail: How interpretation is provided is the accessibility lead's call.

items.title: The copy on channel two.
items.body: After the briefing, the template's history explains channel two: last month, with the interpreter off sick, someone set audio 2 to ‘program (copy)’ as a temporary fix. She came back the next week. The ‘temporary’ didn't leave. And the camera preset ‘PODIUM TIGHT’ was saved in 2019 — two years before the interpreter's position was added to the room.
items.label: Test: how many households — and who signs off the framing?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Amara and Maya beside a board. The Spanish channel is carrying English, and the interpreter's cropped out of the stream picture. And the broadcast partners say our feed is ten dB hot. They take it at minus twenty-four. People who need the second language or the interpreter are getting the worst version.

bubbles.text: The Spanish channel is carrying English, and the interpreter's cropped out of the stream picture.
And the broadcast partners say our feed is ten dB hot. They take it at minus twenty-four.
People who need the second language or the interpreter are getting the worst version.

items.caption: Mastery: nobody hands you the tool. Pick it, and say why.

items.label: **Find it:** where did the Spanish go?

items.alt: A briefing sheet: the stream's 16:9 picture framed tight on the podium with the interpreter cut off at the left edge; beside it a checklist — audio 1 English; audio 2 a copy of the English program; interpreter outside the saved framing; captions verbatim; the partner feed at −14 LUFS when partners take −24; video 200 ms behind audio.
items.caption: Four ways to shut people out.

items.title: ‘audio 2: program (copy) — temp’
items.body: The stream template's change history: ‘Audio 2 source → Program (copy) — temp, interpreter off sick.’ Dated last month. The interpreter came back the next week. The ‘temp’ didn't leave.

items.title: Words on the screen
items.body: In 1972 an American public television station broadcast a cooking programme with open captions — words burned into the picture — so that deaf viewers could follow a national programme as it aired, for one of the first times. Closed captions, which viewers could switch on themselves, followed in 1980. Each step came from people asking to be counted in the audience.

items.title: Two hundred milliseconds.
items.body: Two complaints remain. A partner station says the feed is ten decibels hot; they take −24 LUFS and the county sends −14. And viewers who lip-read — and the interpreter herself, watching the monitor — say the speech runs ahead of the lips: the new encoder's picture processing puts video 200 ms behind the audio.
items.label: Test: how much delay — and how much gain?

items.prompt: Partners want −24; the picture is 200 ms late. What's the fix?
items.risk: Partners dropping the feed; lip-readers and the interpreter out of time.
timeout: Tomorrow's briefing goes out the same way.

options.label: Turn the podium mics down 10 dB
options.result: The partners are happy; the stream is now too quiet for everyone else.
options.consequence: Fixes one feed by breaking the other.

options.label: Partner feeds through loudness processors set for −24; audio delayed 200 ms to match the picture; checked at a partner's receiver and on a phone; a new camera preset with the interpreter saved
options.result: Partners confirm −24. Lips and speech land together on the phone. The new preset is named ‘PODIUM + INTERPRETER’.
options.consequence: Each feed at its own target, and time put back where the picture lost it.

options.label: Ask the partners to fix it at their end
options.result: Three stations, three different fixes, none of them checked.
options.consequence: Hands your path to other people.

options.label: Speed the video up instead
options.result: Encoders don't run backwards in time.
options.consequence: The picture's delay can't be removed — the audio waits for it.

items.label: **Fix it:** Spanish on its own channel, partners at their loudness.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #107 · AVERY'S LENS  Accessible is part of ‘working’  A public briefing works only if everyone it's for can follow it: the second language on its own channel, the interpreter in the picture, captions, the right loudness and lips in time — checked before every briefing.  A county's flood briefing streamed English on its Spanish channel, cropped out its sign-language interpreter and ran speech ahead of the lips.

items.alt: The briefing sheet after the fix: the stream picture wider, the interpreter fully in frame beside the podium; every checklist row green — English on audio 1, the Spanish interpreter on audio 2, the interpreter in every shot, captions verbatim, the partner feed at −24 LUFS, audio delayed 200 ms.
items.caption: Everyone it's for.

items.prompt: Everyone always says ‘we'll sort the access after’. After never comes.

options.label: “Then it isn't after. It's a checklist before every briefing, and it's yours to sign.”
options.reply: Mine to sign. I like the sound of that.

options.label: “It's a technical problem.”
options.reply: It's a people problem with a technical symptom.

items.prompt: Who makes sure every briefing is accessible from now on?
items.risk: The next ‘temporary’ change shutting people out again.

hints.text: Would this still be checked if you weren't here?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S11E06). Option B needs Team at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Check it when someone complains
options.result: The next complaint arrives mid-briefing, again.

options.label: A pre-briefing accessibility checklist — Spanish channel, interpreter in frame, captions, partner loudness, lip sync — run at 16:50 by a trained operator and signed off by Amara
options.result: Friday at 16:55 every line is green, and Amara signs it.
options.consequence: Checked every time, by someone trained, signed by the owner.

options.label: You check it yourself before every briefing
options.result: It works while you're in the building.
options.consequence: The best you can do without a trained operator — and it depends on you.

options.label: Trust the saved template
options.result: The template is how this happened.

items.alt: The briefing room after Friday's briefing; Amara holds the signed checklist; Imogen with her notes in two languages.

bubbles.text: Every line green at 16:55. Mine to sign — and I signed it.
Two viewers wrote in to say thank you. In Spanish.

items.title: ‘PODIUM TIGHT · saved 2019’
items.body: The briefing camera's presets: ‘PODIUM TIGHT — saved 2019.’ The interpreter's position was added to the room in 2021. Nobody re-saved the shot.

items.alt: The EOC at night during the second storm; Kit, arriving with a bag over his shoulder, points at the clock; Maya, pale and tired, at the radio desk.

bubbles.text: You've been on since six yesterday. Maya — that's sixteen hours.
I know the gateway. Nobody else does.

items.caption: Next: *Hour Sixteen.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A briefing works only if everyone it’s for can follow it: the second language on its own channel, the interpreter always in frame, captions verbatim, partners at their loudness (G = target − measured), speech in time with lips (D = video − audio latency). Fix what’s yours live, with the owners; then make it repeatable with a checklist run by a trained operator and signed by the accessibility lead.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Who is in your audience that your checks don’t include?
